source.title: CXR-LanIC: Language-Grounded Interpretable Classifier for Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
source.authors: Yi-Ming Tang; W. Zhong; Rushi Shah; Dianbo Liu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It contains page-break artifacts and an inconsistency about whether pattern annotation and validation have been completed; the experiments section says annotation and explanation validation are planned.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses sparse transcoder neurons as interpretable features in a medical-image classifier, but does not test the claim versions about language-model neuron interpretability or the stated challenges to it.
record.gate_note: The paper reports approximately 5,000 curated patterns from transcoder neurons, but this is for a chest-X-ray classifier, not a test of the specified claim versions. Its stated ≥80% held-out agreement criterion is a filtering rule, not a reported validation result; explanation validation is described as planned. The reported average diagnostic accuracy of 0.88 does not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains transcoders, a learned replacement dictionary, on a chest-X-ray classifier. It curates their latents and plans LMM labelling from activation exemplars, the method of the second original source. It never measures the share of a model's own neurons with one job and never scores explanations against held-out activations. It also does not test pose-type misreadings or native-neuron circuits. None of V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors present CXR-LanIC as transcoder-based pattern discovery on a BiomedCLIP classifier. They report about 5,000 patterns and competitive accuracy (0.88 average), with each prediction decomposing into 20–50 patterns. They conclude that medical imaging models can be accurate and interpretable. They also concede the patterns currently lack natural-language descriptions, and that LMM annotation and radiologist validation are planned.
record.recipe_differences: The paper applies an ensemble of sparse transcoders to a task-trained BiomedCLIP chest-X-ray classifier and aims to curate clinical image patterns; it does not reproduce the cited language-model neuron audit or explanation-scoring procedures.

fits_no_version.finding: About 5,000 transcoder latents, out of 1.5 million candidates from a 100-transcoder ensemble, were kept after qualitative, frequency and clinical-relevance filtering. They span six clinical categories. No validation of their interpretations is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse transcoder latents trained on a task-specific chest-X-ray classifier's penultimate embeddings can be curated into thousands of clinically categorized patterns.

record.problems: The paper gives no reported independent validation outcomes for the pattern interpretations; explanation validation is planned. The abstract and method describe pattern interpretation as accomplished, while the experiments and conclusion say natural-language annotation and validation are still planned.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported outcomes directly test the listed claim versions. In particular, the average diagnostic accuracy of 0.88 is not a measure of neuron interpretability or explanation quality.

untested.parts: Whole version: no audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or their shares.
Whole version: no language models, dense or mixture-of-experts, and no scale comparison.
Whole version: no InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron reanalysis.
Whole version: no comparison of native-neuron interpretability across architectures, regularization or tools.
Whole version: no attribution graphs on native neurons. The study uses trained transcoders instead.
Whole version: no test of whether exemplar-based explanations predict activations. Validation is only planned.
Whole version: no simulation-based scoring of explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's 'monosemantic' label for the patterns is asserted, not measured. Curation is partly manual and selects for clinical relevance, so 5,000 out of 1.5 million (about 0.3%) is not a share of interpretable units. The paper is internally inconsistent: the method describes Claude labelling as done, while the experiments say it is planned, and curated counts differ (500–1000 vs 5,000). The general reliance on LMM labelling of exemplars echoes the second original source, which the paper cites only in passing.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and its reported shares of one-job, two-related-job, and not-yet-understood neuron poles.
Comparisons across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, and model scale up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Whether architecture, regularization, and tools explain messy late-layer neurons, or whether interpretability shares rise from about 5% to about 99% in InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Whether attribution graphs using a large model's own neurons explain behavior without a trained replacement model and its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples fail to predict where neurons fire.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text and the share of neurons with good scores.

rows.subject: BiomedCLIP diagnostic classifier
rows.operation_detail: Curated transcoder-neuron patterns using activation examples and clinical-pattern criteria.

conditions.value: activation consistency, discriminative power, and clinical relevance

rows.value: approximately 5,000 patterns; cardiac (800), pulmonary (1,500), pleural (600), structural (1,200), device (400), and artifact (500)
rows.note: The paper says this count follows filtering of 1.5 million candidate transcoder neurons. Curation includes qualitative inspection, report-text similarity, and manual review; the paper does not report an independent validation result for the pattern interpretations.
rows.check: This is a selection count, not a measured result. The 5,000 patterns are transcoder latents filtered by qualitative inspection, frequency (0.1–50%) and clinical relevance, not the classifier's own neurons. The count therefore cannot be read as an interpretability share. The method section also gives a different figure: 'approximately 500-1000 high-quality interpretable patterns'. The stated '≥80% agreement' criterion has no reported outcome.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
